Mishel Franklin Desilva
Smoke testing
● Smoke testing is a quick, preliminary test suite designed to verify that the core functionalities
of a new build are working before more extensive testing begin.
● It is a subset of acceptance testing. And the term “smoke testing” comes from the hardware
testing practice of turning on a new piece of hardware for the first time and considering it a
success if it does not catch fire or smoke.
● The objective of smoke testing is to verify the “stability” of the system.
When to do smoke testing?
● When a new build/version is deployed to Staging or Pre-production or Code merge
● Before Major Testing Phases like, regression testing, user acceptance testing (UAT), or
performance testing,
● Before Demonstrations or Reviews.

-- 6 of 20 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Sanity testing
● Sanity testing is a software testing process that verifies the core functionality of a software
application after making minor changes or bug fixes
● It is a subset of regression testing
● Unlike smoke testing, sanity testing is more focused and in-depth, concentrating on specific
functionalities rather than the entire application.
When to do sanity testing?
● When a new build/version is deployed to Staging or Pre-production or Code merge
● After Bug Fixes or Minor Code Changes
● When a new feature is build

-- 7 of 20 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Regression testing
● Regression testing is a process that ensures that new changes, like bug fixes or new
features, haven't introduced any unexpected issues or broken existing functionality.
● It involves re-running tests that previously passed to verify that the software still works as
expected after changes.
● It is focused on thoroughness and attention to detail, involving the execution of all existing
test cases and scenarios
When to do regression testing?
● When new functionality is added to the system and the code has been modified
● When some defect has been identified in the software and the code is debugged to fix it.
● When the code is modified to optimize its working.

-- 8 of 20 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Exploratory testing/Ad-hoc testing
● Exploratory testing is a software testing approach where testers actively explore a system,
identifying issues and assessing user experience without relying on pre-written test cases.
● SQA or testers use their learning, knowledge, skills, and abilities to test the software
● Exploratory testing was first named “ad-hoc testing”. The “exploratory testing” was named by
the software testing expert Cem Kaner in the classic book, Testing Computer Software.
When to do exploratory testing?
● When a new tester joins and needs to learn quickly about the application and provide rapid
feedback.
● when there is a need to review products from a user perspective.
● When to ensure that the tester doesn’t miss the edge cases that can lead to critical quality
failures.

-- 9 of 20 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
System testing
● System testing, also known as end-to-end testing,
● System testing evaluates the complete and integrated system to ensure it meets specified
requirements.
● System testing is performed after integration testing and involves testing the entire
application as a whole to ensure that all components work together correctly
When to do system testing?
● When to cover the end-to-end functions of a system, and to provide reliability to the system
● When to test the entire system architecture as per the business requirement.
● When to simulates real-world scenarios to identify defects and confirm that the software
behaves as expected in a production-like environment

-- 10 of 20 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Acceptance testing / UAT (User Acceptance
Testing)
● Acceptance testing is a crucial phase of testing where the final product is evaluated by
end-users or stakeholders to ensure that it meets all the requirements and is ready for
deployment.
● It verifies whether the software functions as planned, meets user expectations, and aligns
with business goals.
● Essentially, it's the "go/no-go" decision point where the customer validates the product's
suitability before release.
When to do acceptance testing?
● When to find the defects missed during the functional testing phase.
● When to improve the product performance and real user experience.
● When to minimize or eliminate the issues arising from the production.

-- 11 of 20 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Integration testing
● Integration testing verifies how separate modules or components of a software application
interact and work together as a cohesive unit.
● It ensures that data flows correctly between these modules and that the combined
functionality meets the overall system requirements.
● Imagine you have several building blocks. Integration testing is like putting those blocks
together to see if they fit and work correctly as a structure, not just individually.
When to do integration testing?
● When to to identify any bug that arise when different components are combined and interact
with each other
● When to verify that the expected sequence is followed.

-- 12 of 20 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Full Cycle testing
● Full Cycle Testing means performing continuous testing across all phases of the Software
Development Life Cycle (SDLC) — including planning, design, development, deployment,
and maintenance.
○ It validates that the software meets both functional and non-functional requirements at
every stage.
○ It ensures that data flows correctly between these modules and that the combined
functionality meets the overall system requirements.
● Imagine you have several building blocks. Integration testing is like putting those blocks
together to see if they fit and work correctly as a structure, not just individually.
When to do Full Cycle Testing?
● From the beginning to end of SDLC
● When to verify covers all types: reviews requirements, unit, integration, system, acceptance,
regression, etc.
● That entire ongoing process — from idea to post-release validation — is Full Cycle Testing.

-- 13 of 20 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Few More Testing Techniques
● End-to-End Testing (E2E): Testing the complete workflow of an application from the user’s
perspective; from start to finish.
● Alpha Testing: Internal testing conducted by the development or QA team before releasing
the software to external users. It is done in a controlled environment to catch bugs early.
● Beta Testing: External testing conducted by real users or a limited audience outside the
development team. It is done in the real-world environment to gather feedback and identify
issues that weren’t caught internally.
● Compatibility Testing: Ensures the application works on different browsers, devices, OS,
or hardware.
● Usability Testing: Tests the application’s user-friendliness.

content:
📝 Types of Software Testing
1. Functional Testing (What the system does)
● Ensures features work as described in requirements.
● Focus: Inputs, outputs, and business logic.
● Examples:
○ Enter valid login → user should log in.
○ Fill registration form → account is created.
○ Search for “shoes” → shows shoe products.
2. Non-Functional Testing (How the system performs/feels)
● Checks quality attributes: speed, usability, reliability, scalability.
Speed → System responds quickly
Example: Google Search delivers results in under 1 second.
Usability → System is easy and intuitive to use
Example: Instagram’s interface is simple and user-friendly.
Reliability → System works consistently without failures
Example: Online banking transfers always complete successfully.
Scalability → System can handle growth and high demand
Example: Amazon handles millions of users during Black Friday without crashing.

-- 1 of 5 --

3. Black Box Testing (No code access)
● Tester has no knowledge of internal code.
● Focus is only on input/output and visible behavior.
● Examples:
○ Enter wrong password → error message should appear.
○ Upload invalid file → system should reject it.
4. White Box Testing (Code-level)
● Tester has full access to code.
● Focus is on internal logic, loops, branches, and coverage.
● Examples:
○ Test all if/else conditions in a tax calculation function.
○ Ensure exceptions are handled properly in code.
5. Grey Box Testing (Some code knowledge)
● Tester has partial knowledge of system design or architecture.
● Combines user perspective (black box) with system knowledge (white box).
● Examples:
○ Login testing knowing passwords are stored as hashes.
○ Testing checkout knowing discount rules are applied in the database.

-- 2 of 5 --

6. System Testing (End-to-End)
● Validates the entire system as a whole.
● Checks integration of all modules.
● Example: User flow → Login → Search → Add to Cart → Checkout → Logout.
7. Acceptance Testing (UAT – Final check by client/user)
● Performed to ensure system meets business requirements.
● Usually done by client or end user before release.
● Example: A school tests its student registration system: form fill → OTP → confirmation
email → client approves.
8. Regression Testing (Re-check old features after changes)
● Makes sure new code changes don’t break existing functionality.
● Often automated for efficiency.
● Examples:
○ After fixing a bug in checkout, re-test login, cart, and payment.
○ After adding a new feature, ensure old features still work.
9. Smoke vs Sanity Testing
● Smoke Testing: Quick, broad check → Is the build stable for testing?
○ Example: App opens, login works, dashboard loads.

-- 3 of 5 --

● Sanity Testing: Narrow, focused check after a fix → Does the change work?
○ Example: OTP bug fixed → test OTP entry, resend, and verification.
10. Exploratory Testing (Unscripted)
● A testing approach where learning, test design, and execution are carried out
simultaneously. Curiosity, creativity, and discovery are emphasized. The system is
explored as it might be by a real user, without being restricted by predefined test cases.
● Useful when time is short or documentation is missing.
● Examples:
○ Sort a product list by price and verify the order.
○ Submit a form while disconnecting the internet mid-submit, then reconnecting.
11. Integration Testing (Modules working together)
Checks how different modules or components interact with each other.
Focus: Data flow, communication, and interfaces between modules.
Examples:
● Login module passes user ID → Profile module loads correct data.
● Payment module connects with Bank API → transaction is successful.
● Shopping cart updates correctly after adding/removing items.
✅ Quick Recap
● Functional: Does the feature work?

-- 4 of 5 --

● Non-Functional: How well does it work?
● Black Box: No code knowledge.
● White Box: Full code access.
● Grey Box: Partial knowledge.
● System: End-to-end testing.
● Acceptance: Client’s final approval.
● Regression: Old features still work after changes.
● Smoke: Is build testable?
● Sanity: Is fix working?
● Exploratory: Creative, unscripted testing.

Principles of Software
Testing
SQA: Manual &
Automated Testing

-- 1 of 19 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Background
● Software testing is a crucial part of the software development process, making sure that
products are robust, functional, and up to users' needs and desires.
● But still, testing is more than simply verifying whether "everything works", it requires
performing it efficiently and effectively
● It is important that you achieve optimum test results while conducting software testing
without deviating from the goal
● But how you determine that you are following the right strategy for testing?
● For that, you need to stick to some basic testing principles.
● There are the common seven testing principles that are widely practiced in the software
industry.

-- 2 of 19 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Software Testing Principles: At a glance

-- 3 of 19 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Principle 1: Testing shows the presence of
defects
● 	Testing can prove the presence of defects.
● 	Deviations discovered while testing show a failure.
● 	The cause of the failure might not be obvious.
● 	Testing reduces the probability of defects remaining undiscovered.
● The absence of failure does not prove the correctness of the software.
● 	The test procedure itself might contain error
● 	The test conditions might be unsuitable for finding errors.

-- 4 of 19 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Principle 2: Exhaustive testing is not possible
● Exhaustive testing: A test approach in which the test suite comprises all combinations of
input values and preconditions
● Test case explosion: Defines the exponential increase of efforts and costs when testing
exhaustively
● Sample test: The test includes only a (systematically or randomly derived) subset of all
possible input values
● Under real life conditions, sample tests are generally used.
● Testing all combination of inputs and preconditions is only economically feasible in
trivial case

-- 5 of 19 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Principle 3: Early testing
● The earlier a defect is discovered, the less costly is its correction.
● 	Highest cost effectiveness when errors are corrected before implementation
● 	Concepts and specifications may already be tested.
● 	Defects discovered at the conception phase are corrected with the least effort & costs.
● 	Preparing a test is time consuming as well.
● 	Testing involves more than just test execution.
● 	Test activities can be prepared before software development is completed.
● 	Testing activities (including reviews) should run in parallel to software specification
and design.

-- 6 of 19 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Principle 4: Defect clustering
● Find a defect and you will find more defects nearby!
● 	Defects often appear clustered like mushrooms or cockroaches
● 	It is worth screening the same module where one defect was found
● 	Testers must be flexible
● 	Once a defect is found it is a good idea to reconsider the direction of further testing.
● 	The location of a defect might be screened at higher detail level, e.g. starting
additional tests or modifying existing tests.

-- 7 of 19 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Principle 5: Pesticide paradox
● Repeating tests under the same conditions is ineffective.
○ Each test case should contain a unique combination of input parameters
○ For a signal test objects, otherwise no additional information can be gained.
○ 	If the same tests are repeated over and over again, no new bugs can be found
● 	Tests must be revised regularly for different code modules.
○ It is necessary to repeat a test after changes have been made in the code (bug fixing,
new functionality).
○ Automating tests can be an advantage if a group of tests cases is used regularly.

-- 8 of 19 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Principle 6: Testing is context dependent
● Testing is done differently in different contexts
● Different test objects are tested differently.
● The engine controller of a car requires tests different than those of an ecommerce
application
● Test environmental (test bed) vs. production environment
● Test take place on an environment other than the production environment.
● The test environment should be very similar to the production environment.
● 	There will always be deviations between test environment and the production
environment. These deviations impeach the conclusions drawn after testing.

-- 9 of 19 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Principle 7: Absence of errors fallacy
● Successful testing find the most serious failure
● In most cases, testing will find all defects of the system (see principle 2), but the most
serious defects should be found.
● This alone does not prove the quality of the software.
● The functionality of the software may not meet the needs and expectations of the
users.
● You can not test quality into the product, it must be built in from the very beginning!

-- 10 of 19 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Summary:
● Tests can help finding defects in the software, however; they can not give proof of the
absence of defects
● For non-trivial system, exhaustive testing is impossible, sample testing necessary.
● Early testing helps reduce costs because defects discovered early on are fixed with
less effort
● 	Defects show up clustered. Finding a defect at one place will mean you probably find
another defect nearby.
● 	Repeating identical tests produces no new information
● 	Each particular environmental determines the way in which tests will run
● 	Error-free software does not imply suitability for use.

-- 11 of 19 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Human Psychology and Testing
● The software that we work on applies a humanistic approach that necessitates human
participation at every level.
● And the software is always created, tested, and also most of the time, used and misused
by humans.
● Therefore, it takes a great deal of work and understanding to be ready to accept the reality
of our human error.
● Thus, several psychological elements affect productivity and testing.

-- 12 of 19 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Different mindset with Example
● We work constructively toward the software during development with the goal of satisfying
client needs. On the other hand, we search for flaws in the product when we test or
examine it.
● Example: Imagine working as a chef in a five-star establishment. Using the ingredients at
hand, it is your responsibility to prepare the greatest meal you can. From your perspective,
the meal is perfect because you bring all of your expertise to the table. Imagine now that
the hotel has employed an internal quality inspector to sample your food and report back
to the hotel management on its flavor and quality.
● The mindset of a quality inspector can be related with that of a tester, and the mindset of a
chef with that of a developer. While the chef prepares the cuisine with good intentions, the
quality inspector checks the dish for errors or defects.

-- 13 of 19 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Characteristics of a Software Tester
● Software testing and software development are concurrent processes. Both seek to fulfill
predetermined criteria and objectives to meet client’s expectations
● But 	there 	are 	difference 	towards 	working 	procedure.
● Software development is a creative or constructive act. Software testing, on the other
hand, 	typically 	falls 	under 	the 	negative 	or 	destructive 	work 	category.
● Furthermore, software testing has developed methods and approaches that are intended
to maximize a tester's ability to identify flaws.

-- 14 of 19 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Skills in addition to technical skills
● Interpersonal skills: First and foremost, testers and developers should communicate
clearly, completely, humbly, and comfortably regarding flaws, failures, test outcomes, test
progress, risks, etc.
● Sharp observation: An "eye for detail" is the second requirement for software testers. If
the testers pay close attention, they can easily spot or notice a lot of critical problems.
● Destructive creativity: The tester must also acquire destructive talents. The tester should
not "hesitate to do negative testing". Checking the system in unexpected circumstances is
known as negative testing. Example: If a login ID is designed to only contain letters, for
example, the tester should also test it with numbers and special characters.
● Customer-oriented perspective: The QAs/Testers should be able to test the product as
an end-user and put themselves in the shoes of the consumer.

-- 15 of 19 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
● Ironical but friendly: The tester needs to be determined in challenging even the smallest
ambiguity until it is proven, regardless of the project's nature. During the test, various
scenarios could occur. This relationship needs to be balanced by the tester. Errors
shouldn't be made in the process. The goal of "attacking software issues but not software
developers" should be defended and persuaded by testers.
● Organized, flexible, and patient at work: Testers should realize that they can also make
mistakes. They should therefore be very good at organizing; they also need to have
checklists, data, and statistics to back up their conclusions. The tester should also be
adaptable and receptive to new procedures. The software should be retested for as many
potential new faults as the tester is patient enough to do. In projects where requirements
change 	frequently, 	testers 	need 	to 	be 	patient 	and 	stay 	organized.
● Objective and neutral attitude: In a software project, testers are like bad news bearers.
When the tester is accused of performing his job (i.e., identifying faults) too well, he must
be able to handle the situation. The development team should recognize the tester's
efforts and accept the mistakes. Because every possible issue the tester may find would
result in a smaller chance of a issue the client could have found.

-- 16 of 19 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
How to improve communication
● Effective communication is one of the major competencies of a tester, in addition to
technical and the domain knowledge. Moreover, they must to be able to establish a
pleasant relationship with their coworkers, particularly with their development team.
○ Do not boast - You're not perfect either!
○ Do not blame - the errors are probably from the group instead of an individual.
○ Be constructively critical and discuss the defect and steps to reproduce it.
● Discuss how to fix the defect so that the delivered system is better for the client.
○ Do not just see the pessimistic side, praise the efforts as well.
○ Show discovered risks and the benefits of fixing the defects.
○ Confirm that the developer has understood the defect clearly
● Collaborate instead of battling around. Everyone in the project has a common
objective of creating better software.
○ Be collaborative, kind, and helpful to your colleagues
○ Try to understand how the other person feels and why he/she reacts the way they do.

-- 17 of 19 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Roles and responsibilities
Developer’s Role 	Tester’s Role
● Implements requirements 	● Plans testing activities
● Developers structures 	● Design test case
● Design and programs the software 	● Is concerned only with finding defects
● Creating a product is his success 	● Finding errors made by a developer is the
success
● Ensures that the final product is closely aligned
with customer expectations
● Ensures that newly written code has less bugs
before it goes into production/live/deployment
● Generally comprises unit tests. 	● Generally comprises multiple tests –
regression tests, accessibility tests, usability
tests, performance tests, stress tests, etc.

-- 18 of 19 --

Mishel Franklin Desilva
Any Questions?
Thank you!

Definition
● BRD (Business Requirements Document): High-level, business-focused.
Defines why the feature exists, business goals, stakeholders, scope, constraints.
● PRD (Product Requirements Document): Defines what the feature must do
from a product/user perspective—user stories, functional & non-functional
features, acceptance criteria, release criteria.
● SRS (Software Requirements Specification): Technical specs that detail how
the system must behave—detailed functional and non-functional requirements,
use cases, interface definitions, assumptions.
Quick Comparison Table
Document 	Focus / Audience 	Key Role in Login Module
BRD 	Why — Business
stakeholders
Sets business goals (retention,
compliance), scope, ROI (Return on

acceptance, release criteria

-- 1 of 6 --

Document Examples for a Log in Module
A. BRD – Business Requirements Document
1. Executive Summary
The goal is to provide secure access to registered users via a login feature, improving user
engagement and retention.
2. Business Objectives
● Increase user retention by 20% within 3 months.
● Ensure only registered users access protected content.
3. Scope (In-Scope / Out-of-Scope)
● In-Scope: Email/password login, “Forgot Password”.
● Out-of-Scope: Social login options (e.g., Google, Facebook), two-factor authentication.
4. Stakeholders
● Product Manager (vision & metrics)
● Business Analyst (requirements gathering)
● Security Officer (compliance)
● Development & QA teams
5. Constraints / Assumptions / Risks
● Must comply with GDPR and local data laws.
● Timeline: MVP in 4 weeks.
● Risk: Weak password enforcement could expose vulnerability.
6. Benefits & Cost-Benefit Analysis
● Benefit: Better user security → lower churn.
● Cost: ~200 development hours; expected ROI via increased engagement outweighs
cost.

-- 2 of 6 --

B. PRD – Product Requirements Document
1. Purpose & Goals
Enable users to log in securely to their accounts using email and password to access
personalized features.
2. Target Audience
● Users: Returning users needing access.
● Internal: Developers, UX designers, QA.
3. Features / Requirements
● User Story: As a returning user, I want to log in using my email and password so that I
can access my account.
○ Functional Requirements:
■ Accept email & password, authenticate.
■ Provide “Forgot Password” link.
■ Display error messages for invalid credentials.
○ Non-Functional Requirements:
■ Response time ≤ 2 seconds.
■ System up ≥ 99.9% availability.
■ Secure transmission (SSL/TLS).
4. Use Cases / Flow
● Basic login, failed login attempts, password reset workflow.
5. Acceptance Criteria
● Login success returns a user dashboard.
● Invalid attempt shows “invalid credentials”.
● Password reset email is sent within 2 minutes.

-- 3 of 6 --

6. Release Criteria
● Functionality passes all test cases.
● Meets performance and security standards (e.g., OWASP basics).
7. Timeline & Milestones
● Week 1: UI/UX prototype
● Week 2: Backend authentication
● Week 3: End-to-end integration + testing
● Week 4: Bug fixes and release

-- 4 of 6 --

C. SRS – Software Requirements Specification
1. Introduction
● Purpose: Provide detailed spec for login behavior to guide developers.
● Definitions / Acronyms: SSO, JWT, TLS, etc.
2. Overall Description
● System context: Client web app interacts with authentication API.
● Assumptions: User registry exists, email service operational.
3. Functional Requirements
● FR-1: System must validate credentials against user database.
● FR-2: On successful login, system issues JWT valid for 24 hours.
● FR-3: On login failure, return HTTP 401 error.
● FR-4: “Forgot Password” triggers email with secure reset link (expires in 1 hour).
4. Non-Functional Requirements
● Performance: Login API ≤ 2 s 95% of the time.
● Security: TLS 1.2+, hashed passwords (bcrypt), rate limit login attempts, audit logs.
● Reliability: 99.9% uptime for authentication gateway.
● Scalability: Support 500 concurrent login requests per second.
5. External Interfaces
● User Interface: Login form (email/password), error message placeholders.
● APIs:
○ POST /login → request: email/password; response: JWT.

-- 5 of 6 --

○ POST /forgot-password → request: email; response: 200 OK.
○ POST /reset-password → request: token + new password; validate token,
reset.
6. Data Requirements
● User table: email, hashed_password, last_login_at.
● Login attempts table: user_id, timestamp, IP address.
7. Use Cases / Diagrams
● Use case diagram for login, reset flow; sequence diagrams.
8. Assumptions / Dependencies
● Dependency on SMTP service for reset emails.
● The User table must support email indexing.

Software Testing Lifecycle (STLC)
🔹 1. What is STLC?
● STLC = Software Testing Life Cycle
● A step-by-step process testers follow to ensure software works correctly.
● Analogy:
○ SDLC → Cooking the dish (developers build it).
○ STLC → Tasting the dish (testers check quality).
🔹 2. Difference: SDLC vs STLC
● SDLC: Build the software (done by developers).
● STLC: Test the software (done by QA/testers).
● Example:
○ SDLC → Developer builds login page.
○ STLC → Tester checks login with valid, invalid, empty inputs.
🔹 3. Phases of STLC
1. Requirement Analysis – Understand what to test.
👉 Ex: “Login should allow only registered users.”
2. Test Planning – Define scope, strategy, tools, and schedule.

-- 1 of 5 --

3. Test Case Design – Write step-by-step test cases.
👉 Ex: Enter correct email + password → expect success.
4. Environment Setup – Prepare servers, devices, test data.
5. Test Execution – Run test cases, mark Pass/Fail/Blocked.
6. Defect Reporting – Log bugs when expected ≠ actual.
7. Test Closure – Summarize results, share lessons learned.
🔹 4. Test Environment Setup
● Prepare hardware, software, tools, network, test data.
● Steps:
1. Define requirements (OS, DB, browser).
2. Install & configure.
3. Load test data.
4. Verify stability.
🔹 5. Test Execution
● Run designed test cases → compare actual vs expected.
● Mark status: Pass / Fail / Blocked / Not Run.
● Failures → reported as defects.

-- 2 of 5 --

🔹 6. Traceability Matrix (TM)
● Definition: A table mapping requirements ↔ test cases.
● Ensures complete coverage.
● Example:
Requirement ID 	Requirement Description 	Test Case ID Statu
s
R-01 	User must log in with valid creds 	TC-01, TC-02 Pass
R-02 	Wrong password should show
error
TC-03 	Fail
R-03 	Password cannot be blank 	TC-04 	Pass
🔹 7. Defect Lifecycle
1. New → Tester reports bug.
2. Assigned → Developer gets it.
3. Open / In Progress → Developer fixing.
4. Fixed → Developer claims issue resolved.
5. Retest → QA retests the fix.
6. Closed → QA confirms resolved.
7. Reopened → Bug still exists.
8. Deferred / Rejected → Fix postponed or bug invalid.

-- 3 of 5 --

🔹 8. Test Cycle Closure
● Done at the end of a sprint/release.
● Conditions: Exit criteria met, no critical bugs open.
● Deliverables: Test summary, metrics, lessons learned.
🔹 9. Exit Criteria & Evaluation
● Predefined rules for ending testing.
● Examples:
○ 100% test cases executed.
○ 95% passed.
○ No high-severity bugs open.
🔹 10. Test Closure Activities
● Create summary report.
● Collect metrics (coverage, defect density).
● Archive test cases & results.
● Share lessons learned.

-- 4 of 5 --

🔹 11. Test Plan, Test Cases & Checklists
📄 Test Plan
● A roadmap for testing: scope, strategy, timeline, environment.
📝 Test Case Example
● Title: Verify login with valid credentials.
● Steps: Enter email + password → Click login.
● Expected Result: User logs in successfully.
✅ Test Checklist Example (Login)
● Login works with valid credentials.
● Wrong credentials blocked.
● Empty fields blocked.
● Special characters handled.
✅ Wrap-up
● SDLC builds software, STLC tests it.
● Phases: Requirement → Planning → Design → Setup → Execution → Defect Reporting
→ Closure.
● Defect lifecycle ensures bugs are tracked till resolution.
● Traceability Matrix & Checklists prevent gaps in testing.
● Early QA involvement saves cost and effort.

Software Development Life Cycle & Agile
Methods
1. What is SDLC?
● Definition: A structured process that defines how software is developed, tested, and
maintained.
● Importance:
○ Provides a clear roadmap for development.
○ Ensures quality and predictable outcomes.
○ Helps teams manage risks, time, and costs.
○ Encourages documentation and accountability.
2. Phases of SDLC
1. Requirement Analysis – Gather and document what the client needs.
Example: An e-commerce app must allow product search & checkout.
2. Design – System and UI design, database schema.
Example: Wireframes of product catalog, ER diagram for inventory.
3. Implementation (Coding) – Developers build the system.
4. Testing – QA verifies functionality, usability, performance, and security.
5. Deployment – Software is released to production.
6. Maintenance – Fixing bugs, upgrades, new features.

-- 1 of 6 --

3. Waterfall Model
● Flow: Sequential → Requirement → Design → Implementation → Testing →
Deployment → Maintenance.
● Characteristics: Each stage must be completed before moving on.
✅ Pros:
● Simple to understand and manage.
● Good for projects with fixed requirements.
● Clear milestones.
❌ Cons:
● Changes are difficult once development begins.
● Testing comes late → higher risk of late defect detection.
● Not flexible for evolving requirements.
📌 When to Use:
● Banking, government, defense, and large corporate projects where requirements are
stable.
󰠁 QA Involvement:
● Mostly in the Testing phase, not much influence in early phases.

-- 2 of 6 --

4. V-Model (Verification & Validation Model)
● Extension of Waterfall where testing activities run in parallel with development
phases.
● Flow:
○ Requirement Analysis ↔ Acceptance Testing
○ System Design ↔ System Testing
○ Architecture Design ↔ Integration Testing
○ Module Design ↔ Unit Testing
✅ Pros:
● Early defect detection since test planning starts early.
● Ensures quality at each stage.
❌ Cons:
● Still rigid, changes are costly.
● Not suitable for dynamic projects.
5. Agile Process
● Why Agile? Designed for projects where requirements change frequently.
● Agile Manifesto Values:
○ Individuals & interactions > processes & tools
○ Working software > comprehensive documentation
○ Customer collaboration > contract negotiation

-- 3 of 6 --

○ Responding to change > following a plan
● Agile vs Waterfall:
○ Agile: Iterative, flexible, early delivery.
○ Waterfall: Linear, rigid, late delivery.
6. Scrum Framework (Agile Methodology)
● Roles:
1. Scrum Master – Facilitates team, removes blockers.
2. Product Owner – Manages backlog, prioritizes requirements.
3. Development Team – Builds the product.
● Ceremonies:
1. Sprint Planning – Define sprint goal and backlog.
2. Daily Stand-up – 15-min status check.
3. Sprint Review – Demonstrate product to stakeholders.
4. Sprint Retrospective – Team reflects and improves process.
● Sprint Lifecycle:
Product Backlog → Sprint Planning → Sprint Execution (2–4 weeks) → Review →
Retrospective.
󰠁 QA in Scrum:
● Involved from the start.
● Works alongside developers in every sprint.
● Performs continuous testing and automation.

-- 4 of 6 --

✅ Benefits:
● Adapts to changes quickly.
● Early delivery of working features.
● Higher customer satisfaction.
7. Kanban (Agile Methodology)
● Visual workflow management system.
● Columns: To Do → In Progress → Done.
● Principle: Continuous delivery, no time-boxed sprints.
● Best for: Support/maintenance projects or continuous flow of tasks.
8. Agile Work Hierarchy
● Project → Online Shopping App
● Epic → Shopping Cart
● Story → As a user, I want to add items to my cart
● Task → Build “Add to Cart” button
● Sub-task → Code button function, test it
👉 Flow: Project → Epic → Story → Task → Sub-task

9. Story Points (Agile Estimation)
● Definition: A relative measure of effort/complexity to implement a user story.
● Why: Focuses on effort, complexity, and risk instead of exact time.
● Estimated Using: Fibonacci sequence (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13...).
📌 Example:
● Simple Login button → 2 story points.
● Search with filters + sorting → 8 story points.
● Multi-step checkout with payment integration → 13 story points.
👉 Teams use story points to calculate velocity/time (how many points completed per sprint).
